lead: This unit is the core of supervised learning: fit a model, define its loss, train it, and judge it honestly. After it you can derive least-squares and logistic regression, run batch or stochastic gradient descent, diagnose bias and variance, apply ridge or lasso, and choose a model with cross-validation and the right metric.
about: The unit starts with 2.1, linear regression by least squares for one and many inputs. 2.2 turns the fitted line into an optimisation problem: loss functions and batch or stochastic gradient descent. 2.3 changes the output to a probability with logistic regression, and 2.4 generalises the score to binary and multiclass linear classifiers. 2.5 explains why a flexible model can fail on new data through overfitting, underfitting and the bias-variance trade-off. 2.6 controls that failure with ridge and lasso penalties. 2.7 closes with cross-validation, evaluation metrics and model selection, the practical loop that chooses among all earlier models.

chapters.idea: A linear model predicts a numeric target as a weighted sum of inputs, and least squares picks the weights that minimise squared error.
chapters.depth: Cover simple linear regression y = b0 + b1x and multiple regression y = b0 + Σ bj xj. Show residuals, SSE, MSE, the matrix form y = Xw + e, and the normal equation w = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy. Include polynomial regression as linear regression on powers x, x², and so on. Some syllabi call multiple linear regression multivariate regression. Nonlinear least squares is only a few universities teach it; keep it to one short note.

figure.aria: Scatter points for five students lie exactly on the least-squares line marks = 2 times hours + 1.

chapters.example: Study hours x = 1,2,3,4,5 and marks y = 3,5,7,9,11. Find the least-squares line. Means x̄ = 3, ȳ = 7; Sxy = Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ) = 20; Sxx = 10; b1 = 20/10 = 2; b0 = 7 − 2×3 = 1; line marks = 2×hours + 1. Predict 6 hours: 13 marks.
chapters.trap: Using R² alone to claim a good model; a high R² on training data can come from overfitting, and extrapolating far outside the observed x is unsafe.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 math review: vectors, matrices, mean, variance, summation.
chapters.leave: R² and cross-validated error to 2.7; gradient training to 2.2; overfitting to 2.5.

chapters.idea: Training is minimisation: choose a loss that measures error, then move parameters downhill along the gradient.
chapters.depth: Cover MSE and SSE, MAE, why squared error is common, convex loss, gradient, learning rate α, batch gradient descent, stochastic gradient descent, mini-batch, epoch, shuffling, convergence, and feature scaling. Show the update w := w − α ∂J/∂w. Some syllabi call batch gradient descent steepest descent.

figure.aria: A convex loss curve with five gradient-descent updates moving from w = 0 toward the minimum at w = 3.

chapters.example: Minimise J(w) = (w−3)² + 2 with α = 0.2 from w0 = 0. Gradient 2(w−3). Update w1 = 0 − 0.2×2(0−3) = 1.2; w2 = 1.2 − 0.2×2(1.2−3) = 1.92; w3 = 2.352. The minimum is w = 3.
chapters.trap: A learning rate too large overshoots or diverges; too small stalls. Forgetting that SGD computes the gradient from one example, so its path is noisy.
chapters.leave: Logistic loss to 2.3; backpropagation and optimisers to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Logistic regression turns a linear score into a probability and classifies by a threshold, usually 0.5.
chapters.depth: Cover sigmoid σ(z) = 1/(1+e^−z), log-odds log(p/(1−p)) = w·x + b, maximum likelihood giving binary cross-entropy loss, decision boundary, and the threshold as a separate choice. Mention multiclass softmax as a pointer to 2.4. Some syllabi call it the logit model.

figure.aria: Sigmoid curve for z = −5 + 2x crosses 0.5 at x = 2.5, with marked probabilities at x = 1 and x = 3.

chapters.example: With z = −5 + 2x, find p at x = 3 and the boundary. p = 1/(1+e^{−1}) = 0.731. Boundary p = 0.5 when z = 0, so x = 2.5. At x = 1, p = 1/(1+e^{3}) = 0.047.
chapters.trap: Fitting by least squares on 0/1 labels instead of maximising likelihood; also reading p as a hard class. The threshold is a choice, not part of the fitted probability.
chapters.prereq: 2.1 linear score, 2.2 gradient descent; Unit 1 probability.
chapters.leave: Naive Bayes and generative models to Unit 3; neural network activation to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A linear classifier assigns the class whose linear discriminant function has the largest score.
chapters.depth: Cover discriminant g_i(x) = w_i·x + b_i, binary sign rule, multiclass argmax, one-vs-rest, one-vs-one, decision boundaries, and linear separability. Include a least-squares classifier that fits ±1 targets by regression. Some syllabi call these linear discriminant functions. Perceptron training is Unit 5; maximum margin and kernels are Unit 3; LDA is Unit 4.

figure.aria: Line 2x1 + 3x2 = 6 separates a positive point at (2,1) from a negative point at (0,0).

chapters.example: Binary score g(x) = 2x1 + 3x2 − 6. Boundary 2x1 + 3x2 = 6. For x = (2,1), g = 4 + 3 − 6 = 1 > 0 so class +. For x = (0,0), g = −6 so class −. For three classes with scores g1 = 0.2, g2 = 1.1, g3 = −0.4, predict class 2.
chapters.trap: Comparing raw scores across differently scaled features or forgetting the bias term; in multiclass, one-vs-rest scores are not probabilities and need not sum to 1.
chapters.leave: Perceptron training to Unit 5; SVM maximum margin and kernels to Unit 3; LDA to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A model can memorise training noise (overfit) or miss the pattern (underfit); bias-variance explains the trade-off.
chapters.depth: Cover training versus validation error, model complexity, dataset size, learning curves, and the decomposition E[(y−f̂)²] = bias² + variance + σ², where σ² is irreducible noise. Underfitting has high bias; overfitting has high variance. Some syllabi call this the bias-variance dilemma.

figure.aria: Training error falls as polynomial degree rises, while validation error is lowest at degree 3 and rises sharply at degree 9.

chapters.example: Eight points from a smooth curve. Degree-1 polynomial: train MSE 4.2, validation MSE 4.5. Degree-3: train 1.1, validation 1.4. Degree-9: train 0.01, validation 6.8. Choose degree 3; degree 1 underfits, degree 9 overfits.
chapters.trap: Judging overfitting by training error; training error almost always falls as complexity rises. The validation curve, not the training curve, shows the turning point.

chapters.idea: Regularization adds a penalty on weight size to reduce variance and prevent overfitting.
chapters.depth: Cover ridge L2 penalty λΣw_j², lasso L1 penalty λΣ|w_j|, objective = loss + penalty, tuning λ, feature scaling, ridge closed form w = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy, lasso sparsity and soft threshold, and a one-line mention of elastic net. Some syllabi call ridge L2 regularization and lasso L1 regularization.

figure.aria: As λ rises, ridge shrinks w smoothly from 3, while lasso falls linearly and reaches zero at λ = 3.

chapters.example: One weight has unregularized w = 3 and λ = 1. Ridge minimises ½(w−3)² + ½λw², giving w = 3/(1+λ) = 1.5. Lasso minimises ½(w−3)² + λ|w|, giving soft threshold w = sign(3)max(|3|−1,0) = 2. Lasso shrinks more and can set weights to zero.
chapters.trap: Regularizing the bias term; also comparing λ values without scaling features, so the penalty unfairly shrinks large-scale features.
chapters.leave: Cross-validated choice of λ to 2.7; feature selection and LDA to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Cross-validation estimates generalisation error, and metrics turn errors into the numbers used to choose a model.
chapters.depth: Cover train/validation/test splits, k-fold cross-validation, stratified folds, leave-one-out, regression metrics MAE, MSE, RMSE and R², and classification metrics from the confusion matrix: accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1, ROC/AUC. Include model selection, class imbalance, and a one-line warning on domain shift. Some syllabi call this model assessment.

figure.aria: Five-fold cross-validation splits the data, trains on four folds, tests on the fifth, and averages the five scores.

chapters.trap: Tuning on the test set, or reporting accuracy on imbalanced data; a 95% accurate classifier can miss every positive case. Use the validation folds for choices and touch the test set once.
chapters.leave: Clustering evaluation to Unit 4; ensembling to Unit 3.

links: least-squares error becomes the loss minimised by gradient descent
the same gradient method trains logistic weights
logistic score is one linear discriminant
extra features can overfit a linear model
CV selects the learning rate and epochs
